# From research question to interpretation {#sec-rq-to-interpretation}

In September 1967, the British government began a crackdown on drunk driving: police could now stop drivers and test their breath.^[The study of this crackdown, by Ross, Campbell, and Glass, is a classic of the genre; @shadish2002 use it as a showcase. The details in this section follow their account.] In the months that followed, traffic casualties dropped. Ministers were pleased, newspapers reported success, and you can already feel the question forming: *did* the crackdown save lives, or did the numbers just happen to go down?

This chapter is about the gap between those two things — a number that moved, and a question that got answered. Every empirical study, however simple or however fashionable, is an argument that some numbers computed from data answer a question about the world. Once you can see the structure of that argument, you can read any study — a clinical trial, a survey, a machine learning benchmark — and ask the same few questions of it. You will also be able to design studies whose arguments hold up.

## The chain from question to answer

Here is the structure in one picture:

![The chain from research question to interpretation. The design makes the assumptions plausible; the assumptions define the model; the model turns data into results; and the results answer the question only as far as the assumptions hold.](diagrams/chain.png){#fig-chain width="45%" fig-align="center"}

In words: a **research question** motivates a **research design** — a plan for which data to collect and how. The design does something subtle and crucial: it makes a set of **assumptions** plausible. Those assumptions, taken together, are the **model**. Fitting the model to the data gives **results** — estimates, intervals, predictions. And the results answer the research question, *to the extent that the assumptions hold*.

That last clause is the whole point of this chapter, so let me say it again differently. The numbers that come out of an analysis are just numbers. They become an answer to a question about the world only through the assumptions, and the assumptions are believable only because of the design. A regression coefficient from a randomized experiment and the numerically identical coefficient from a volunteer web survey are different objects — different assumptions stand behind them.

The Breathalyzer researchers understood this. They did not just observe that casualties fell; they asked *when* they fell. If the crackdown did the work, casualties should drop most during weekend nights — pub closing hours — and hardly at all on weekday mornings. That is exactly the pattern they found, and series on miles driven and on alcohol sales helped rule out the boring explanations (people driving less, drinking less). The number moved *and* it moved in the specific pattern the causal story demanded. Design features did the convincing; the arithmetic only kept score.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 1.1"}
A newspaper reports: "People who drink moderate amounts of red wine live longer, a study of 50,000 adults finds." Without knowing anything else, write down (a) the research question the study presumably wants to answer, and (b) one assumption that must hold for the finding to answer that question.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 1.1"}
(a) Presumably: *does moderate red wine consumption cause longer life?* Nobody changes their behavior over a mere association. (b) That drinkers and non-drinkers are comparable in every other respect that affects longevity — income, health, social life. Nothing about observing 50,000 adults makes that plausible: wealthier, healthier people drink wine at different rates than others. This assumption of "no confounding" will follow us through the whole book.
:::

## Research questions

Research questions come in three recognizably different kinds, and the difference matters because each kind demands different things from design and model [@shmueli2010; @hofman2021].

A **descriptive** question asks what the world looks like: *what proportion of Dutch adults had depressive symptoms last year? How much does income vary between neighborhoods?* Description does not ask why.

An **explanatory** — or plainly, *causal* — question asks what would happen if we changed something: *does exercise reduce depressive symptoms? Did the Breathalyzer crackdown reduce casualties?* The tell-tale sign is a hidden "if we intervened." And here we should be precise about what an "effect" even is. An effect is a comparison of the world with the treatment against the same world without it — in the words of @shadish2002, the difference between what did happen and what would have happened. That second world is a "counterfactual": contrary to fact, unobservable in principle. We never see September 1967 without the crackdown. A central task of all cause-probing research is to construct a believable stand-in for that missing world, and to understand exactly how the stand-in differs from the real thing.

A **predictive** question asks what will happen, or what is the case, for units we have not observed: *which patients will miss their appointment next week? Is this email spam?* Prediction does not ask why either. A variable can predict superbly without causing anything — ashtrays predict lung cancer.

It is tempting to think these are three flavors of the same activity, so that a model good at one is good at the others. They are not, and it is not. Shmueli [-@shmueli2010] shows that explanation and prediction pull model-building decisions in different directions at every step, and that a theoretically "wrong" model can predict *better* than the true one.^[The reason is a trade-off we will meet properly in the machine learning chapters: prediction error has a bias part and a variance part, and accepting some bias — a simpler, wrong model — can buy a large reduction in variance. Also, a cause is not always usable for prediction: characteristics of a wine barrel may explain quality after the fact, but cannot predict this year's quality "if at the time of prediction the grapes are still on the vine" [@shmueli2010].] Conversely, an accurate predictor may explain nothing. The most useful habit is also the simplest: **first identify which kind of question is being asked.** The same fitted equation — the same $y = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + \dots$ — can be descriptive, explanatory, or predictive depending on how it is used and read [@hofman2021]. The question, not the technique, determines what kind of study you are looking at.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 1.2"}
Classify as descriptive, explanatory, or predictive: (a) Does mandatory quarantine reduce influenza transmission? (b) How many students drop out of secondary school in Utrecht each year? (c) Which loan applicants will default? (d) Do students who use AI tools learn less? (e) Among patients presenting with chest pain, who is having a heart attack?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 1.2"}
(a) Explanatory. (b) Descriptive. (c) Predictive. (d) Explanatory — the causal claim hides in "learn less *because of the tools*"; an association between use and learning would be merely descriptive. (e) Predictive (diagnostic): we want a current unknown state, not the consequence of an intervention.
:::

## Research designs

A **research design** is a plan for producing data: whom to measure, what to measure, when — and above all, who gets exposed to what, and how that was decided. Some designs are purposeful: the researcher controls data collection, as in an experiment, whose defining feature is that something is deliberately varied to discover what happens to something else [@shadish2002]. In other studies the data simply arrive — administrative records, routine care data, social media traces — and the "design" is whatever process happened to generate them. Found data still have a design; you just did not choose it, and you will have to reconstruct what it was.

Some designs you will meet repeatedly:

- **The randomized experiment.** Units — people, schools, plots of land — are assigned to conditions by a coin flip, and outcomes are compared. In medicine this is the "randomized controlled trial" (RCT), the gold standard for treatment evaluation.
- **The cross-over experiment.** Each unit receives *both* conditions, in randomized order, serving as its own control.
- **Two groups, before and after.** One group becomes exposed (to a policy, say), another does not; both are measured before and after, and we compare the *changes*. Economists call the comparison "difference-in-differences"; in the older methodological literature this is the "nonequivalent comparison group design", the most common quasi-experiment of all [@shadish2002].
- **The interrupted time series.** Many measurements before and after a known intervention moment — the Breathalyzer design. The long pre-intervention series projects what would have happened without the intervention.
- **The regression discontinuity.** Units are assigned to treatment purely by a cutoff on some score (a means test, an exam grade); the effect shows up as a jump in outcomes at the cutoff.
- **The cohort study.** A group is followed over time; exposures and outcomes are recorded as they occur, without intervention.
- **The case–control study.** Units are sampled *on the outcome* — cases with the disease, controls without — and we look back at their exposures.
- **The probability sample survey.** Units are drawn from a population by a known chance mechanism and measured.
- **The convenience sample.** Whoever was available: students in the hallway, volunteers on a website.
- **The natural experiment.** Nature or bureaucracy assigns exposure — an earthquake, a lottery, an arbitrary rule — and the researcher argues the assignment was as good as random.

The names matter less than what each design *buys*, which is the business of the section after next. First, the other half of the chain.

## Models are sets of assumptions

The word "model" gets used loosely, so let me fix a definition and stick to it:

> A **model** is a set of assumptions about the process that generated the data.

Every analysis has a model in this sense, whether or not anyone wrote it down. Compute a mean with a confidence interval, and you have assumed observations drawn independently from some population. Fit a linear regression and you have assumed — at least — that the relationship is linear; read its coefficients causally and you have assumed a great deal more. Train a random forest to predict dropout and you have assumed next year's students resemble the ones you trained on.

Statistical and machine learning methods are, in this view, models plus recipes for fitting them. A few that appear in this book and its sequels:

| Model | Typical question it serves |
|---|---|
| Linear regression | How does a numeric outcome relate to predictors? |
| Logistic regression | How does a yes/no outcome relate to predictors? |
| Analysis of variance (ANOVA) | Do group means differ? How much variation does each factor contribute? |
| Factor analysis, item response theory (IRT) | What do many related measurements have in common? |
| Hidden Markov model | How does an unobserved state evolve over time? |
| Gaussian process | What smooth function could have produced these points? |
| Random forests, neural networks (including transformers) | What is the best prediction of the outcome, functional form unknown? |

: A few models and the questions they typically serve. Every entry is a set of assumptions — the fashionable ones too. {#tbl-models}

Two remarks about @tbl-models. First, no entry is exempt: a transformer trained to predict the next word embodies assumptions (that deployment data resemble training data, among others) just as surely as a *t*-test does. Second, no entry is intrinsically "causal" or "not causal". Whether a model's output answers a causal question is decided by assumptions that come from *outside* the arithmetic — from the design. The same regression can live a descriptive, an explanatory, or a predictive life [@hofman2021].

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 1.3"}
A hospital trains a model on last year's records to predict which arriving patients will need intensive care, planning to use it next year. Name two assumptions this makes — one about time, one about use.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 1.3"}
Time: next year's patients, treatments, and record-keeping resemble last year's; a new triage policy or a new virus breaks this. Use: acting on the predictions must not change the process — if staff treat flagged patients earlier, the sensor-to-outcome relationship the model learned starts to shift under its feet. Neither assumption shows up in the accuracy metrics. Both come from thinking about the design: how the data arose and how the predictions will be deployed.
:::

## What a design is for

Now the central idea of this chapter, and really of the book. **The purpose of a research design is to make the assumptions of the model plausible.**

To see how, it helps to borrow some vocabulary. Methodologists call the ways an inference can go wrong "threats to validity", and the classic catalogue is @shadish2002. A few threats to the claim "the treatment caused the difference we see":

- *Selection.* The groups being compared differed to begin with, in ways that also affect the outcome.
- *History.* Something else happened at the same time as the treatment.
- *Maturation.* People were already changing — growing older, healing, learning — and would have changed without treatment.
- *Regression artifacts.* Units selected for extreme scores drift back toward the middle when measured again, mimicking an effect.^[This one artifact explains a remarkable share of everyday miracles: patients who seek therapy at their lowest point improve; last season's worst team does better after firing its coach. Extremes tend not to repeat.]
- *Attrition.* People drop out, unevenly across groups, after the study starts.

Each design feature exists to disarm specific threats — that is what design features are *for*:

- **Randomized assignment** disarms selection. In the words of @shadish2002, randomization "equates groups on expectations of every variable before treatment, whether observed or not." Not on the observed values — on expectations; the luck of the draw guarantees the groups differ only by chance, including on everything nobody thought to measure. This is the assumption of **no confounding**, purchased by a coin flip.
- **A comparison group** disarms shared history and maturation: whatever else was going on, it was going on for both groups.
- **A pre-measurement** in both groups reveals initial differences and lets us compare *changes* — at the price of a new assumption, that the groups would have changed in parallel without treatment.
- **A long pre-intervention series** (the Breathalyzer design) disarms maturation and regression artifacts by putting the trend on display; its remaining weak spot is history — something else happening at the intervention moment — which the pub-hours pattern was recruited to address.
- **A cross-over design** removes stable differences between persons entirely, and charges for it: the new assumption that the first condition does not linger into the second ("no carry-over").

Notice the pattern, because it never goes away: *designs do not eliminate assumptions; they trade implausible assumptions for more plausible ones.* When a design feature is missing, the corresponding assumption does not disappear. It just stands there, unsupported. You can still compare wine drinkers with non-drinkers; you are then *assuming* comparability rather than *arranging* it, and the strength of your study is the strength of that assumption's defense.

Let us watch the central case happen — in simulation, where we know the truth. Suppose exercising has *no effect whatsoever* on depressive symptoms, but motivated people both exercise more and feel better.

```{r}
#| label: fig-confounding
#| fig-cap: "The same true (zero) effect of exercise on symptoms, estimated in 1000 simulated observational studies (left) and 1000 randomized experiments (right). Vertical line: the truth."
set.seed(1)

one_study <- function(randomized) {
  n <- 300
  motivation <- rnorm(n)                          # never measured
  if (randomized) {
    exercise <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)                 # coin flip
  } else {
    exercise <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(motivation))  # the motivated exercise
  }
  symptoms <- 10 - 1.5 * motivation + 0 * exercise + rnorm(n)
  coef(lm(symptoms ~ exercise))["exercise"]
}

obs <- replicate(1000, one_study(randomized = FALSE))
rct <- replicate(1000, one_study(randomized = TRUE))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(obs, main = "Observational", xlab = "Estimated effect",
     xlim = c(-2, 1), breaks = 30); abline(v = 0, lwd = 2)
hist(rct, main = "Randomized", xlab = "Estimated effect",
     xlim = c(-2, 1), breaks = 30); abline(v = 0, lwd = 2)
```

The first command defines one simulated study: motivation drives symptoms, and — in the observational version only — motivation also drives who exercises. The `replicate` calls run a thousand of each. Look at the left panel: the observational studies find, again and again, that exercise "reduces" symptoms by more than a full point. This is not bad luck in one sample; the estimates pile up in the wrong place. That is **bias**, and more data would only make us more precisely wrong. On the right, randomization has severed the link between motivation and exercise, and the estimates pile up around the truth.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 1.4"}
Modify the simulation so exercise *also* truly reduces symptoms by 0.5 points. Predict what both histograms will show before you run it; then run it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 1.4"}
Change `0 * exercise` to `-0.5 * exercise`. The randomized histogram centers on $-0.5$, the truth. The observational one centers near $-1.7$: the real effect plus the confounding bias. The observational study gets the direction right for the wrong reason and overstates the size threefold. Confounding does not announce whether it is inventing an effect or exaggerating one.
:::

## Within the study, and beyond it

Confounding is about comparisons *within* the data. A second family of assumptions is about reaching *beyond* them: for whom does the answer hold?

If units enter the sample by a known chance mechanism — a probability sample — then sample statistics estimate population quantities, uncertainty and all. That is what random sampling is *for*. If units enter by convenience, the assumption "these people behave like the population I care about" must stand on its own; sometimes it can (basic visual perception is probably similar in students and everyone else), sometimes it cannot (political attitudes of hallway volunteers). Note that the two chance mechanisms do different jobs: **random assignment supports causal comparison within the study; random sampling supports generalization beyond it.** They are often confused because both contain the word "random", and almost never present together — random sampling is rarely feasible in experiments [@shadish2002]. Hence a fair summary of most of science: experiments are highly local but have general aspirations. A perfectly randomized trial on volunteers answers its causal question — for people like the volunteers. Whether the answer travels is a further argument, resting on knowing *why* the effect occurs and what it needs to operate.^[There is an art to that argument — @shadish2002 devote a third of their book to it. When you must have it, the short version: ask what features of the people, treatment, outcome, and setting the causal relationship depends on, and whether the new situation shares them.]

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 1.5"}
An online panel of 2 million self-registered users is weighted so its age, gender, and education distribution matches the country's. It is then used to estimate national vaccine hesitancy. What assumption replaces random sampling, and how could it fail?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 1.5"}
The assumption: within each age–gender–education cell, panel volunteers have the same hesitancy as their demographic twins outside the panel. It fails if the kind of person who joins internet panels differs in outcome-relevant ways — trust in institutions, say, which travels with vaccination attitudes. Weighting fixes only the composition you can see, and the panel's size is no defense: two million biased respondents estimate the wrong number very precisely.
:::

## Exploratory and confirmatory research

So far the chain ran forwards: question, then design, then model. Often research runs backwards. You have data — perhaps collected for something else — you notice a pattern, and only then do you formulate the question to which the pattern is the answer. This is **exploratory** research, and it is how many good ideas are born; unexpected findings tangential to the original aim have repeatedly been the source of major advances [@shadish2002].

Exploratory research is not bad. What is bad is *pretending it was confirmatory*. The pretense is not cosmetic; it invalidates the model. A $p$-value of .05 means: results this extreme occur by chance one time in twenty *when this single test was fixed in advance*. Run twenty tests and report the best, and the relevant chance — of finding *something* this extreme — is .64; at fifty tests it is .92 [@shadish2002]. The design that justified the error rates ("I will test this one hypothesis") never happened. Statisticians call this "fishing"; the polite term is that the analysis had many "researcher degrees of freedom". And prediction is not immune: with free choice of task, metric, and data cleaning, the same model on the same data can be made to look extremely accurate or barely better than guessing [@hofman2017]. Any analysis flexible enough to find something is flexible enough to find nothing in particular.

The honest options are simple to state. Label exploration as exploration — legitimate the moment it is clearly described as such [@shadish2002]. Or better: let the exploratory data *generate* the question, and fresh data — a new sample, a preregistered replication, a held-out test set never touched during exploration — *answer* it [@hofman2017]. Then the chain of this chapter is restored: the question exists before the design that answers it.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 1.6"}
A team studying diet and health measures 120 food items and 40 health outcomes, and reports: "Yogurt consumption was significantly associated with lower blood pressure ($p = 0.01$)." In what way might this be exploratory research pretending to be confirmatory, and what happens to the meaning of that $p$-value?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 1.6"}
There are $120 \times 40 = 4800$ item–outcome pairs; about 48 of them will show $p \le .01$ by pure chance even if nothing is going on. If yogurt–blood-pressure was noticed *because* it stood out, "results this extreme occur by chance only 1% of the time" no longer describes what happened — the chance of finding *some* pair this extreme was near certainty. The search was a fine way to generate the yogurt hypothesis. Answering it takes new data, or an analysis that honestly accounts for the search.
:::

## Reading a study: five questions

The learning goals of this chapter fit in a checklist. For any study — including your own — ask:

1. **What is the research question?** Often unstated or vague; reconstruct it, and classify it: descriptive, explanatory, predictive.
2. **What is the design?** Who was measured, how were they selected, who was exposed to what — and how was *that* decided?
3. **What is the model?** Which analysis was run, and, more important, what assumptions does interpreting its results require?
4. **How do design and model combine into an answer?** Trace the chain: which result answers the question, through which assumptions?
5. **Does the design warrant the assumptions?** For each key assumption, point to the design feature that supports it — or note that none does, and that it rests instead on hope, argument, or adjustment.

The rest of this book is practice in asking these five questions with increasing precision. The next chapter takes the step this one glossed over: how, exactly, do you get from a theory about the world to a *specific* model — with coefficients you can estimate, interpret, and be proven wrong about?

## Test yourself {.unnumbered}

Harder than the inline exercises; comparable to exam questions.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 1.A"}
A study finds that patients treated in high-volume hospitals (many operations of a given type per year) have better surgical outcomes than patients in low-volume hospitals, adjusting for patient age and comorbidity. The authors conclude that concentrating surgery in high-volume centers would improve outcomes.

(a) State the research question the analysis answers and the question the conclusion answers; explain the difference.
(b) Identify the design.
(c) Name the key assumption needed for the analysis to support the conclusion — using this chapter's threat vocabulary — and give one concrete way it fails.
(d) Propose one design change that would make the assumption more plausible, and state what new assumption it introduces.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 1.A"}
(a) The analysis answers a descriptive question: do outcomes differ between hospital types for patients of similar age and comorbidity? The conclusion answers a causal one: would *redirecting patients* improve their outcomes? (b) Observational — a cohort comparison with statistical adjustment; patients reached their hospitals by referral and geography, not by assignment. (c) No confounding beyond the two adjusters — equivalently, no *selection* threat: given age and comorbidity, patients at the two hospital types are comparable in all other outcome-relevant ways. Failure: sicker or poorer patients (in unmeasured ways) end up at low-volume hospitals; or high-volume hospitals decline high-risk cases. (d) Randomize referral among consenting patients in a region: selection is disarmed by design, at the price of new assumptions — generalizability from consenters and participating regions, and that randomized referral itself does not change care. A weaker but practical alternative: exploit quasi-random variation such as differential distance to a high-volume center, which buys the instrumental-variable assumptions of @sec-identification.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 1.B"}
A ministry lets schools opt in to a phone-free policy starting in 2025. Researchers compare the change in test scores from 2024 to 2026 between opt-in schools and the rest, and find scores rose more in opt-in schools.

(a) Name the design.
(b) State the assumption under which the comparison of changes estimates the policy's effect.
(c) Explain how voluntary opt-in threatens it — name the threat and give a scenario.
(d) Scores for 2020–2024 are available. How can they probe the assumption, what would reassure you, and what would not?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 1.B"}
(a) Two groups before/after: the nonequivalent comparison group design; the comparison of changes is a difference-in-differences. (b) Parallel change: absent the policy, opt-in schools' scores would have moved like the others'. (c) *Selection*, interacting with maturation and with regression artifacts. Scenario one: schools opt in when something else is already improving — an energetic new principal bans phones *and* improves teaching. Scenario two: schools opt in after an unusually bad year and rebound toward their usual level regardless (a regression artifact). (d) Compare the groups' 2020–2024 trends. Parallel pre-policy trends are reassuring, though not decisive — divergence could begin at opt-in. Diverging pre-trends, or a dip in opt-in schools just before opting in, would show the assumption failing before the policy even starts.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 1.C"}
"Our deep learning model predicts depression relapse from smartphone sensor data with 91% accuracy, far better than clinicians. Patients flagged by the model should therefore receive preventive treatment."

Using the five questions, write a short assessment (≤200 words) identifying at least three distinct assumptions and classifying each as supported, unsupported, or unknowable from the information given.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 1.C"}
A model answer touches: the question *answered* is predictive; the conclusion is causal ("treating flagged patients prevents relapse") — a different question. Assumptions: (1) stability — accuracy was estimated on data resembling deployment (same population, phones, era); unknowable as stated, unsupported if the 91% is training-sample performance. (2) A sensible baseline — "91% accuracy" is uninformative without the relapse rate: with 9% relapse, "nobody relapses" also scores 91% [@hofman2021]; unsupported as stated. (3) An effective intervention exists for the people the model flags — a causal claim needing its own (experimental) evidence; unsupported. (4) Use-invariance — flagging changes clinician behavior, which changes the learned sensor–relapse relationship; unsupported. The design behind the headline supports, at most, the predictive claim on data like the training data. The recommendation needs assumptions no part of the design makes plausible.
:::
